X32: Guitar, Vocal Effects and a Computer

Plug an electric guitar into the X32 (DI box, the built-in amp simulator, or a modeller), build a processed vocal chain, and connect a Windows computer with Ableton over the X-USB card.

Page numbers are from the Behringer X32 Preliminary User Manual (see Works Cited). The manual covers firmware 2.x, so newer firmware may add things it doesn’t mention.

Electric guitar into the X32

Why not plug it straight in?

The 32 inputs on the back are mic preamps. Their input impedance is 10 kΩ balanced (p. 69), and the six Aux In jacks are 20/40 kΩ line inputs. A passive guitar pickup wants a load many times higher than that. On a 10 kΩ input its treble goes, its level drops, and it sounds thin and dull. The X32 has no instrument (Hi‑Z) input.

Use a DI box. It takes the guitar’s high‑impedance signal and sends a balanced mic‑level signal down an XLR cable into a preamp. This is the same as plugging in a mic. Pedals can go between the guitar and the DI.

Guitar
→
Pedalsoptional
→
DI box¼″ in, XLR out
→
Snake / XLR input
→
X32 channelgain, EQ, comp

Active DIs need phantom power (+48 V on that channel) or a battery. Passive DIs need neither.

Three ways to get a tone

1 · Clean, on the desk alone

Guitar → DI
→
Channel EQ + compressor
→
FX send: reverb / delay / chorus

2 · The X32's own amp simulator

Guitar → DI
→
Channel insertFX slot set to “Insert”
→
Guitar AmpSansAmp‑style, cab sim
→
EQ, sends

3 · An amp modeller in front of the desk

Guitar
→
ModellerHelix, Tonex, Boss GT…
→
XLR / line out
→
X32 channel
  1. Clean. The guitar goes through a DI with channel EQ and compression, plus some reverb on an FX send. It works for clean jazz, funk and acoustic‑style parts, but gives no distortion.
  2. The built‑in amp. The effects rack has a Stereo / Dual Guitar Amp “modeled after the Tech 21 SansAmp”, which “allows an electric guitar player to sound great without using an amp on stage” (p. 25). Its controls are Preamp, Buzz, Punch, Crunch, Drive, Low, High and Level, and a Cabinet simulation you can switch off. There is also a Tube Stage for milder overdrive. To use it:
    1. Choose an empty FX slot. Slots 5–8 can only be inserts (p. 19).
    2. In the FX screen, set the slot’s source to Insert and load Dual Guitar Amp. The “Dual” version is two mono amps, so one slot can serve two guitars.
    3. Select the guitar channel. On its Config page, use the 6th encoder to pick the insert, for example Ins FX5L, then press the encoder to connect it (p. 31).
  3. A modeller. A floor modeller or amp‑in‑a‑pedal does the amp and cabinet itself and sends a finished tone into the desk. Most have an XLR or balanced line output, so they need no DI. Turn off the modeller’s cab sim only if a real cabinet is also being miked.

With a real amp on stage, you can still mic the amp’s speaker (an SM57 close to the cone), take a DI split before the amp, or both.

Processed vocals

What the desk does

Mic
→
Gain+48 V for condensers
→

→

→

→

→
Insertde‑esser, pitch
→
FX sendsreverb, delay

Every channel has a gate, a compressor and a parametric EQ. See gates, EQ and compression. The effects rack (60 effects, p. 60) holds most vocal effects:

Effect X32 effect How to use it
Reverb Hall, Plate, Rich Plate, Room, Chamber, Vintage… On an FX send, so several voices share it
Echo / slapback Stereo Delay, 3‑Tap Delay, Rhythm Delay On an FX send, timed to the song by tapping the tempo
Doubling Dual / Stereo Pitch with a few cents of detune and a short delay (p. 25) Insert, or a send for a subtle effect
Octave up or down Dual / Stereo Pitch (±1 octave), Suboctaver Insert. Fixed interval only
Taming “s” sounds Dual / Stereo DeEsser Insert
Warmth / grit Tube Stage, Exciter, Enhancer Insert, used lightly
Radio / telephone voice Channel EQ: cut below ~400 Hz and above ~3 kHz No effect slot needed

What the desk can’t do

The manual lists no pitch correction (Auto‑Tune), no harmoniser that follows the key, and no vocoder. The pitch shifter moves the voice by a fixed interval, so a harmony a third above goes out of key on some notes. For these, add one of:

  • A vocal processor (for example a TC‑Helicon VoiceLive) between the mic and the desk, or on the channel’s insert through an Aux Out and Aux In.
  • The computer (next section).

A Windows computer with Ableton

The X‑USB card

The standard expansion card in the X32 is the X‑USB: one USB 2.0 cable carries 32 channels each way between the desk and a computer, at 44.1 or 48 kHz, 24‑bit (p. 37–42). It also does MIDI and DAW control (Mackie Control / HUI).

Windows: install the X32 ASIO driver from behringer.com (run Setup.exe, p. 40). In Ableton, go to Options → Preferences → Audio, then choose Driver Type ASIO and the X‑USB device, and turn on the input and output channels you need. Mac: no driver is needed (Core Audio).

X32 inputs 1–32
⇄
X‑USB card32 × 32, USB 2.0
⇄
Windows PCX32 ASIO driver
⇄
Ableton Live

On the desk, two routing screens set what goes where:

  • Routing → Card Out chooses what goes to the computer, in banks of 8. Local 1–8 sends the preamps on channels 1–8 (p. 54).
  • Routing → Home chooses what each channel listens to, again in banks of 8: the local preamps or Card 1–8 … 25–32, which are the computer’s outputs (p. 54). Aux In 1–4 can also take Card 1–4 (p. 52).

Four things to do with it

1. Record every channel. Set Card Out to Local 1–32. In Ableton, arm a track per input. A whole band is then on separate tracks for mixing later. The desk’s own USB‑stick recorder only makes a stereo 16‑bit WAV (p. 36), so use the card for multitrack.

2. Virtual soundcheck. Record the band once. Afterwards, switch Routing → Home to the Card banks and play the recording back through the same channels to practise the mix with no band in the room. When a channel listens to the card, its gain knob becomes a ±12 dB trim (p. 39). Save two scenes, “preamps” and “DAW”, so the switch is one recall (p. 39). This is a good way for students to practise the sound check.

3. Ableton as an effects rack. Send a channel to the computer, process it in Ableton, and bring it back on a spare channel:

Guitar / vocal
→
Ch 5 preamp
→
Card Out 5
→
Ableton trackinput 5, monitor In
→
Plug‑insamp sim, Auto‑Tune, vocoder
→
Output 25
→
Ch 25source Card 25–32

Pull channel 5’s fader down, or take it out of the mix, so you hear only the processed return on channel 25. In Ableton, set the track’s Monitor to In, its input to the X‑USB input, and its output to the return channel. Possible plug‑ins:

  • Guitar: Ableton’s Amp and Cabinet (in Suite), Neural DSP, AmpliTube, Guitar Rig.
  • Vocals: Auto‑Tune or other pitch correction, a harmoniser, Ableton’s Vocoder.

4. Backing tracks and a click. Ableton plays stems out of separate card outputs into their own channels, so each one has a fader. Send the click to an output that goes only to the drummer’s monitor or in‑ear mix, never to the main L/R.

Latency: the catch

The desk itself is quick: input to output takes 0.8 ms (p. 69). Going through the computer adds a round trip. The manual gives about 14 ms for the X‑USB, “depending on system performance and application” (p. 42). A performer hears their own voice or guitar late. Below about 10 ms most people don’t notice, but past 15–20 ms it feels like playing in an echo.

  • In the X‑USB control panel (Settings) and in Ableton, set the ASIO buffer as low as the computer allows without clicks. Try 64, then 128 samples.
  • Use few, light plug‑ins on the live tracks. Some amp sims and pitch correctors add a “lookahead” delay, so use their low‑latency mode.
  • Recording, virtual soundcheck and backing tracks don’t care about latency. Only live processing that a performer hears does.
  • For the lowest delay on a guitar, use the X32’s own Guitar Amp or a modeller pedal and keep the computer for recording.

Quick reference

I want… Do this
A guitar into the desk DI box → XLR input. Never a plain ¼″‑to‑XLR adapter
Distorted guitar with no amp Insert the X32 Guitar Amp effect, or use a modeller pedal
A thicker vocal Pitch effect with a few cents of detune (doubling), plus a plate reverb on a send
Auto‑Tune, a harmoniser or a vocoder A vocal processor, or Ableton through the X‑USB card
To record the whole band X‑USB card, Card Out = Local 1–32, a track per input in Ableton
To practise mixing with no band Virtual soundcheck: Routing → Home → Card, or recall a “DAW” scene

See also: the UR22mkII interface for a smaller setup with one or two inputs.
